phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with a careful estimate.
phases.summary: In April 2023, university researchers tried to work out how much water ChatGPT might use. Their answer was about half a litre for a whole conversation, not for one question.

phases.label: How it spread
phases.headline: Then the bottle travelled, and the conversation shrank to one question.
phases.summary: Early stories kept the “whole conversation” detail. Then one headline dropped it, and a bottle per conversation became a bottle per question. That is the version people still repeat.

phases.label: How it was challenged
phases.headline: Then people checked, and the number got much smaller.
phases.summary: The researchers narrowed their own figure. Companies and independent writers then put a single question at a few drops to a few millilitres.

stops.stopTitle: University researchers publish “Making AI Less Thirsty”
stops.whatHappened: Researchers estimate half a litre of water for a whole ChatGPT conversation of 20 to 50 questions.

stops.stopTitle: Gizmodo picks it up
stops.whatHappened: Gizmodo repeats the bottle, still for a whole exchange of questions.

stops.stopTitle: The Associated Press takes it nationwide
stops.whatHappened: The Associated Press spreads it across the US, for a series of 5 to 50 prompts.

stops.stopTitle: Windows Central turns it into a bottle for every query
stops.whatHappened: Windows Central drops the detail: now it is a bottle for every single question.

stops.stopTitle: “One email, one bottle”
stops.whatHappened: A year later, the bottle is pinned to one AI-written email.

stops.stopTitle: The researchers narrow their own figure
stops.whatHappened: The researchers narrow it to the older GPT-3 model and say location matters a lot.

stops.stopTitle: OpenAI’s boss gives a much smaller number
stops.whatHappened: OpenAI’s boss says one question uses about a fifteenth of a teaspoon.

stops.stopTitle: Google publishes its own estimate
stops.whatHappened: Google says a typical prompt uses about five drops.

stops.stopTitle: A writer calls the bottle claim a misconception
stops.whatHappened: A writer estimates about 2 ml per prompt and calls the bottle a misconception.

water.whereItStandsToday: One question uses somewhere between a few drops and a few millilitres, depending on whose estimate you trust. A bottle for every question is not supported. The real issue is local: data centers can strain water in some dry towns on the hottest days.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with a study of what machines could do.
phases.summary: In 2013, two Oxford researchers estimated that 47% of US jobs could technically be automated. It measured what was possible, not a forecast of job losses.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then the estimates got bigger, and the warnings got louder.
phases.summary: After ChatGPT, a bank put a global number on jobs exposed to AI. Then a tech boss said probably none of us will have a job, and the headline dropped the “probably”. An AI company boss added his own warning.

phases.label: How it was checked
phases.headline: Then economists looked at the job data.
phases.summary: Studies found no economy-wide job shock so far, and a leading economist pushed back on the forecasts. The newest data shows an early warning sign for young workers.

stops.whatHappened: Oxford researchers estimate that 47% of US jobs could technically be automated.

stops.whatHappened: Goldman Sachs says generative AI could expose 300 million jobs worldwide to automation.

stops.whatHappened: Anthropic’s CEO warns AI could wipe out half of entry-level office jobs within five years.

stops.stopTitle: Amodei repeats the warning on CNN
stops.whatHappened: He repeats the warning on CNN, saying AI already matches a smart graduate at some tasks.

stops.stopTitle: Yale Budget Lab finds no broad job disruption yet
stops.whatHappened: Yale researchers find no clear sign that AI has disrupted jobs since ChatGPT launched.

stops.whatHappened: An update still shows stability, and asks whether some firms blame AI for layoffs.

jobs.whereItStandsToday: No data shows AI taking all our jobs, or even causing an economy-wide shock so far. The early sign is narrower: young workers in AI-exposed jobs are falling behind, though researchers can’t yet say AI caused it.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with a warning in a philosophy book.
phases.summary: In 2014, Nick Bostrom argued that AI smarter than humans could become extremely powerful, possibly beyond our control. It was a risk to take seriously, not a prediction.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then the warning turned into a prediction.
phases.summary: A 2023 open letter asked AI labs to pause. One writer said that wasn’t enough and predicted everyone on Earth would die. Then a famous AI pioneer quit Google to warn about the dangers, and lab bosses signed a warning about extinction.

phases.label: How experts answered
phases.headline: Then experts answered, and they disagreed.
phases.summary: A leading AI scientist called the fears ridiculous. A large survey of researchers put the typical estimate at about 5%, and a government-backed report found no agreement on how likely it is.

phases.label: Where it went next
phases.headline: Then the prediction became a book title.
phases.summary: In 2025 the claim reached bookshops in its boldest form.

stops.stopTitle: Philosopher Nick Bostrom's book Superintelligence warns AI could escape human control
stops.whatHappened: Philosopher Nick Bostrom warns that superintelligent AI could slip beyond human control.

stops.whatHappened: An open letter asks AI labs to pause their most powerful systems for six months.

stops.whatHappened: Eliezer Yudkowsky says a pause isn’t enough: build superhuman AI and everyone on Earth will die.

stops.whatHappened: Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneer of modern AI, quits Google so he can warn about its dangers.

stops.whatHappened: AI lab bosses and top researchers sign a one-line warning about the risk of extinction.

stops.whatHappened: Meta’s chief AI scientist Yann LeCun calls extinction fears ridiculous.

stops.stopTitle: Survey of 2,778 AI researchers finds a median 5% chance of extinction-level outcomes
stops.whatHappened: A survey of 2,778 AI researchers puts the typical estimate of an extinction-level outcome at 5%.

stops.stopTitle: International AI Safety Report finds experts split on the risk of losing control
stops.whatHappened: An international report finds experts deeply split on the risk of losing control of AI.

stops.whatHappened: Yudkowsky and Soares publish a book called If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.
stops.linkPhrase: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies

existential-risk.whereItStandsToday: Many experts take the risk of losing control of AI seriously, but they disagree about how likely it is. “AI will kill us all” states as certain what most researchers put at a small, uncertain chance.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with one county fight in Virginia.
phases.summary: In 2022, Prince William County opened 2,100 acres next to a Civil War battlefield to data centers, after a 15-hour hearing and loud opposition.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then the costs and benefits were counted.
phases.summary: Virginia’s auditors found big economic benefits and rising power bills. Reports then added up blocked projects, pollution complaints and higher electricity prices across the country.

phases.label: How communities pushed back
phases.headline: Then communities started winning.
phases.summary: In August 2025, Tucson’s council ended a proposed data center, and a judge voided the Virginia zoning from the first stop.

phases.label: Where it stands
phases.headline: Then the fear got its slogan.
phases.summary: In Georgia, an activist warned that data centers “will destroy our community”, and the county kept pausing new projects.

stops.whatHappened: A report counts $64 billion in data center projects blocked or delayed by local opposition.

stops.whatHappened: The NAACP moves to sue Elon Musk’s xAI over turbine pollution in Memphis.

stops.whatHappened: A DeKalb County activist says data centers “will destroy our community”.

stops.whatHappened: DeKalb extends its pause on new data centers, saying it isn’t against technology.

data-centers.whereItStandsToday: Data centers bring real costs, like a constant hum near homes, higher power bills and pressure on water, as well as jobs and tax money. Whether one harms a community depends on where it goes and the rules around it.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with a study, and a headline that went further.
phases.summary: In 2019, researchers estimated the carbon cost of training AI models. A day later, a headline compared one model to five cars, using the study’s most extreme case.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then the tech giants’ own emissions went up.
phases.summary: In 2024, Microsoft and Google both reported rising emissions and linked them to building and powering more data centers.

phases.label: What the forecasts say
phases.headline: Then the forecasts came in.
phases.summary: Government and international reports projected data center electricity use rising fast, while noting that AI could also help cut emissions elsewhere.

phases.label: Where it stands
phases.headline: Then the argument split.
phases.summary: Bill Gates said AI is speeding up clean energy. A historian answered that AI will make climate change worse.

stops.stopTitle: University researchers estimate the energy and carbon cost of training AI language models
stops.whatHappened: Researchers estimate the energy and carbon cost of training AI language models.

stops.whatHappened: Microsoft says its emissions are up 29% since 2020, mainly from new data centers.

stops.stopTitle: Google reports emissions up 48% since 2019, blamed on data center energy use
stops.whatHappened: Google reports emissions up 48% since 2019, tied to data center energy use.

stops.whatHappened: A US government report says data centers could use up to 12% of US electricity by 2028.

stops.whatHappened: The IEA says data center electricity will more than double by 2030, but AI could offset emissions.

stops.stopTitle: Bill Gates says climate change won't end humanity and credits AI with speeding clean energy
stops.whatHappened: Bill Gates says climate change won’t end humanity and AI is speeding up clean energy.

stops.whatHappened: Historian Juan Cole argues AI’s data centers will raise carbon emissions significantly.

energy-climate.whereItStandsToday: AI is pushing up demand for electricity, and where that power comes from gas or coal, emissions rise. How much depends on how fast demand grows and how clean the grid gets, so “will make climate change worse” is too certain.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with artists finding their work inside AI.
phases.summary: In 2022, a fantasy artist learned his name was one of the most used prompts for AI images. Weeks later, artists flooded a big art site with protest posts.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then the objection went to court, and became a slogan.
phases.summary: Artists sued AI image companies for copyright infringement. A philosophy paper then argued that “AI art is theft” holds up as ethics, whatever the law says.

phases.label: How it was answered
phases.headline: Then courts and regulators gave mixed answers.
phases.summary: The US Copyright Office said some AI training is fair use and some isn’t. Hollywood studios sued. A US court allowed training on books but not piracy, and a UK court found an AI model doesn’t store the images it learned from.

stops.whatHappened: The US Copyright Office says some AI training is fair use and some is not.

creativity.whereItStandsToday: Whether AI art is theft is still an argument, not a settled fact. Courts have said training can be legal, but how the training data was obtained can be costly, and many cases are still open.

phases.label: Where it started
phases.headline: It started with a real bug.
phases.summary: In March 2023, a bug let some ChatGPT users see other people’s chat titles. Italy briefly blocked ChatGPT, and OpenAI added a way to turn off chat history and training.

phases.label: How it grew
phases.headline: Then a headline turned training into “sharing your secrets”.
phases.summary: A how-to story told readers ChatGPT was sharing their secrets, when it meant chats being used for training. Days later, Samsung banned staff from ChatGPT after confidential code was pasted into it.

phases.label: Where it stands
phases.headline: Then courts raised new questions, and some got answers.
phases.summary: A court ordered OpenAI to keep deleted chats, and Sam Altman said chats have no legal confidentiality. OpenAI pulled a feature that let shared chats show up in Google, and the court order was later lifted.

privacy.whereItStandsToday: ChatGPT doesn’t show your chats to other people, but they may be used for training unless you turn that off, and they can be handed over in a lawsuit. It’s wise not to share anything you’d need kept truly confidential.
